pull.title: net: limit relative ban times to uint32
pull.body:
`BanMan::Ban` computes the ban end as `GetTime() + bantime` (banman.cpp:140). `setban` and `-bantime` both accept any int64, so a relative bantime close to `INT64_MAX`:

```
setban 1.2.3.5 add 9223372036854775807
```

returns success, but the sum overflows. UBSan reports:

```
src/banman.cpp:140:73: runtime error: signed integer overflow: 1790412558 + 9223372036854775807 cannot be represented in type 'int64_t'
```

Without UBSan the result wraps negative, the ban is treated as already expired, and it is silently dropped. With `-bantime=9223372036854775807` the same happens to every `setban add` that uses the default duration.

This limits relative ban times to uint32 (about 136 years):

- `setban` rejects a relative bantime above `UINT32_MAX` with "Error: bantime is too large"
- `-bantime` is parsed as `uint32_t`, so larger values saturate at `UINT32_MAX`

Absolute timestamps are unchanged.

The added cases in `rpc_setban.py` check that `UINT32_MAX + 1` and `INT64_MAX` are rejected, that `UINT32_MAX` is accepted, and that with `-bantime=INT64_MAX` a default-duration ban is listed with a duration of `UINT32_MAX`. Both parts fail on master and pass with the change. `p2p_disconnect_ban.py` still passes.

AI tools were used to help find this issue and to prepare the patch and test.

I am not sure about starting/trying to support durations that C++ itself doesn't even support (https://en.cppreference.com/cpp/chrono/duration) 

I think it would be fine to reject args that are too large. Though, argparsing doesn't really do any verification and I am sure you can find an int overflow for basically every single arg. Also, `SaturatingAdd` doesn't work for chrono types ...

events.body: Makes sense, switched to rejecting it: setban now fails with "Error: bantime is too large" when a relative bantime wouldn't fit once added to the current time, next to the existing check for absolute timestamps in the past. The SaturatingAdd in BanMan::Ban is gone and -bantime is left as is.

overflows there (UBSan: signed integer overflow in banman.cpp). In

comments.body:
```suggestion
        if (!absolute && banTime > std::numeric_limits<uint32_t>::max()) {
```

This should be more than enough and also avoid the weird time dependency. 

> and -bantime is left as is.

Not sure. I'd say to either fix this fully or not at all. What about parsing it as u32?

Done, took the suggestion: `setban` now rejects a relative bantime above `UINT32_MAX`, and `-bantime` is parsed as `uint32_t` so larger values saturate there instead of overflowing later. The test covers both.

In d49c1c9ab3e139158d76141b71943ff79903e87a

This covers startup args correctly but I think settings.json can also have a value > uint32 which will throw during conversion.

Not sure if that's common enough (or at all) to worry about though.

Good catch, thanks. A bantime above uint32 in settings.json made startup fail with "JSON integer out of range". `-bantime` is now read as int64 again and capped at UINT32_MAX, so it no longer matters where the value comes from. Added a settings.json case to rpc_setban.py, which fails on the previous push. (Changes prepared with AI tools.)
